text: Meridian Finworks runs its loan-origination platform on Azure and its customer-facing API and data lake on AWS. A vendor risk review just flagged weak Conditional Access coverage, a wide-open management port, a wildcard IAM policy, and a Security Group that still allows SSH from anywhere. This lab is the hardening pass a real security engineer runs in response -- identity first, then network, on both clouds.

Step one is Entra ID. The new Conditional Access policy targets Finance-Admins and Loan-Ops-Admins, excludes trusted office and VPN locations, and requires both multi-factor authentication and a compliant device. It goes live in Report-only mode first, so the team can review a full day of sign-in logs and confirm no real admin would have been unexpectedly blocked before switching the policy on.

Step two is the flagged NSG. Its Any-to-Any rule on ports 22 and 3389 gets deleted outright, not narrowed -- a shrunk rule is too easy to widen back open later. In its place, two scoped rules allow only the bastion subnet on those ports, and an explicit deny-all rule at the bottom makes the intent visible to anyone reviewing this NSG next.

Step three is the AWS side: the CI/CD pipeline's deploy role currently holds Action star, Resource star. That gets replaced with the exact actions and resource ARNs the pipeline's own traffic actually uses -- specific EC2, Auto Scaling, and S3 permissions, scoped to the real resources. Running IAM Access Analyzer afterward confirms the earlier wildcard finding on that role is gone.

Step four closes the loop on AWS networking: the Security Group's open SSH rule is replaced with the same bastion and VPN range used on the Azure side, and the application port is locked to accept traffic only from the load balancer's own security group, not the whole VPC. Validation runs Conditional Access's What If tool and a fresh Access Analyzer scan to confirm both fixes actually held.

Lesson 29 hardened identity and network together, assuming nothing had gone wrong yet. Lesson 30 assumes the opposite: a Meridian credential is already in an attacker's hands, and the job becomes detecting it in the Activity Log or CloudTrail, containing it, and remediating it under real time pressure.
